title: Machines: EC2, AMIs and launch templates

story: Nova is building RH-1234 on a full VM, the bigger machine size we use for builds, and like every build it runs the product's tests inside Docker containers. One of those containers runs a test helper that fetches any URL it is given. A poisoned test fixture hands it the address http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/, a special address that exists on every EC2 machine. On a badly configured machine, the helper gets back a JSON document with an access key, a secret and a session token: the VM's role credentials, delivered to a container that should never have had them.
On our VMs the same request gets nothing back. Nobody had to remember to block it on this VM, for this run. The rule was written once, in the one file that every sandbox VM is started from.
hook.question: What decides how every new VM is built, and how does it keep the machine's own credentials away from the code running on it?

read.h: A machine is a size and a disk
p: An EC2 instance is a virtual machine that you rent by the second. Two choices define it. The instance type is its size: a name like m8i.2xlarge reads as family m (general purpose), generation 8, i for an Intel processor, and size 2xlarge, and each size step doubles the processors and the memory. The AMI, an Amazon Machine Image, is the saved disk the machine boots from, with the operating system and every tool already installed. You can think of it as a Docker image for a whole machine, with one difference: it is a complete disk, without layers.

The sandboxes use one AMI, ai-agent-sandbox, rebuilt every night with Docker, Node, Python, git and the product's test setup inside, and three sizes of machine: lite (m8i.xlarge) for plans and small routines, full (m8i.2xlarge) for builds that run the whole product, and wide (m8i.4xlarge) for the heaviest work.

code.file: your terminal, pointed at the practice AWS
code.text:
aws ec2 describe-instance-types \
  --instance-types m8i.xlarge m8i.2xlarge m8i.4xlarge \
  --query 'InstanceTypes[].[InstanceType,VCpuInfo.DefaultVCpus,MemoryInfo.SizeInMiB]' \
  --output text

notes.text: Only three fields: the name, the number of virtual processors and the memory in MiB.

read.h: One recipe for every VM: the launch template
p: Starting a VM means answering many questions: which image, which size, which role, which disk, which tags, which metadata rules. A launch template is a saved set of those answers. The warm pools and the nightly image test start VMs only from the templates, one template per size, so a rule written in the template holds for every sandbox VM without anyone repeating it.

Here is the lite template, written as the JSON that the AWS CLI accepts. Two things are missing on purpose. There is no SSH key, because nobody logs in to a sandbox (a later lesson shows how we send it commands instead). And there is no public address: the VM is placed in the private subnets from the network lesson.

code.file: lt.json (the launch template for lite VMs)

notes.text: Not an AMI ID but a pointer to an SSM parameter, a named value stored in AWS Systems Manager, that holds the ID. Promoting a new nightly image is one write to that parameter.
The instance profile from the IAM lesson: the near-empty role ai-agent-sandbox.
IMDSv2 only: no credentials without a token. The next section explains it.
Hop limit 1: the token cannot reach a container on the VM.
The disk is encrypted, and 120 GiB leaves room for the product's Docker images.
The sweeper finds every sandbox VM by this tag and terminates the ones that were left behind.

deeper.h: Go deeper: versions and the encryption key
p: A launch template has numbered versions. Changing it creates a new version instead of editing the old one, and a group of machines uses either a fixed version or the latest one. That makes a bad change easy to see and easy to undo.

The disk is encrypted with a key from KMS, the AWS key service, that belongs to the sandboxes. The key's policy must allow the role that the Auto Scaling service uses to act for you; if it does not, every launch fails with a key error and the warm pool stays empty.

read.h: The metadata door, and the token that locks it
p: Every EC2 machine can reach a special address, 169.254.169.254, where the instance metadata service, IMDS, answers questions about the machine itself: its ID, its size, and, under iam/security-credentials, the temporary credentials of its role. That is how programs on the VM get the role's credentials without a key on disk. It is also the door from the story: any program that can make an HTTP request to that address can ask.

The first version, IMDSv1, answered any plain GET request, so a test helper tricked into fetching a URL was enough. IMDSv2 adds one step. A program must first send a PUT request to get a short-lived token, and then send that token in a header with every request. Setting HttpTokens to required turns off the old way completely; a plain GET gets 401 Unauthorized. A helper that only follows URLs cannot send a PUT with a special header, so the attack from the story ends there.

The hop limit closes the second gap, containers. Every time a network packet passes through a router, its hop count drops by one, and a packet whose count reaches zero is dropped. With HttpPutResponseHopLimit set to 1, the reply that carries the token survives exactly one hop: enough to reach a program on the VM itself, but not a container behind Docker's network bridge, which is one hop further. So code inside a container never receives a token, even if it knows how to ask for one.

code.file: on a sandbox VM, as a program that is allowed to ask
code.text:
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token \
  -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 300")
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \
  http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/; echo
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' \
  http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/

notes.text: Step one of IMDSv2: a PUT that asks for a token, valid here for 300 seconds.
Step two: every request carries the token in this header. The answer is the role's name.
The IMDSv1 way, a plain GET with no token, for comparison.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the host rules in the image
p: The image adds two firewall rules with iptables, the Linux tool for packet rules. The first lets only root, which runs the SSM agent, reach 169.254.169.254, so Nova's own user, which is not in a container, cannot ask either. The second, in the DOCKER-USER chain, the place Docker reserves for your own rules, drops that address for every container.

These rules are speed bumps rather than walls, because root can delete them and the docker group can become root. The wall behind them is the near-empty role: even if a fooled agent gets the credentials, they can only tell the warm pool that setup is done and talk to Systems Manager.

lab.title: A launch template and a locked metadata door
needs: AWS CLI v2 and the LocalStack image from the p3-1 lab
lab.goal: Write the sandbox launch template on a practice AWS, then use AWS's own metadata mock to see why IMDSv2 keeps the role's credentials from a program that only follows URLs.

guess.q: A launch template sets HttpTokens to required. A test helper on the VM is tricked into a plain GET of http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ai-agent-sandbox. What does it get?

options.text: The credentials, because the request comes from the VM itself.
options.why: That was true with IMDSv1. With tokens required, coming from the VM is not enough: the request also needs a token from a PUT.

options.text: 401 Unauthorized, because the request carries no token.
options.why: IMDSv2 only answers requests that send a token in a header, and a helper that only follows URLs cannot get one.

options.text: Nothing, because the metadata service is turned off.
options.why: HttpEndpoint is still enabled; programs that use the token flow, like the SSM agent, need it.

follow.say: Start LocalStack if it is not running from an earlier lab, and point the AWS CLI at it in a new folder.
follow.do:
docker run --rm -d --name localstack -p 4566:4566 localstack/localstack:4.9 && sleep 15
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p3-3 && cd ~/academy-labs/p3-3 && export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566
follow.see: (a container ID, or a name conflict if LocalStack is already running, which is fine)

follow.say: Compare the three sizes, because the size is the first answer every launch needs.
follow.do: aws ec2 describe-instance-types --instance-types m8i.xlarge m8i.2xlarge m8i.4xlarge --query 'InstanceTypes[].[InstanceType,VCpuInfo.DefaultVCpus,MemoryInfo.SizeInMiB]' --output text

follow.say: Store the current image ID in an SSM parameter, because the template points at the parameter, not at the image.
follow.do: aws ssm put-parameter --name /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id --type String --data-type aws:ec2:image --value ami-03cf127a

follow.say: Create the lite template from the JSON in Understand, and read back its metadata rules.
follow.do:
Save the template from Understand as lt.json, then:
aws ec2 create-launch-template --launch-template-name ai-agents-sandbox-lite --launch-template-data file://lt.json --query 'LaunchTemplate.[LaunchTemplateName,LatestVersionNumber]' --output text
aws ec2 describe-launch-template-versions --launch-template-name ai-agents-sandbox-lite --query 'LaunchTemplateVersions[0].LaunchTemplateData.MetadataOptions'

follow.say: LocalStack does not run a metadata service, so start AWS's own metadata mock, configured like a lite sandbox VM with tokens required. It listens on localhost:1338 instead of 169.254.169.254.
Be the tricked test helper: a plain GET for the role's credentials, with no token.
Now be a program that is allowed to ask, like the SSM agent: get a token with a PUT, then send it with each request.
follow.do:
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X PUT http://localhost:1338/latest/api/token -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 300")
for p in instance-id instance-type iam/security-credentials/; do echo "$p: $(curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" http://localhost:1338/latest/meta-data/$p)"; done
follow.see:
instance-id: i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718
instance-type: m8i.xlarge
iam/security-credentials/: ai-agent-sandbox

lab.build: Write lt-full.json for the full size: the same as lt.json, but with m8i.2xlarge and the tag ai-agents:size set to full. Create the template ai-agents-sandbox-full from it. Then write one describe-launch-template-versions command per template that prints the instance type, HttpTokens and the hop limit, and check that both say required and 1. Last, with the token you already have, read the full credentials document at iam/security-credentials/ai-agent-sandbox and find its Expiration field.
checks: describe-launch-template-versions shows HttpTokens required and HttpPutResponseHopLimit 1 for ai-agents-sandbox-lite.
A plain GET to the mock's credentials path prints HTTP 401.
With a token, the mock answers instance-id, instance-type and the role name ai-agent-sandbox.
ai-agents-sandbox-full exists and prints m8i.2xlarge, required and 1.
You stopped the mock (docker stop imds) and LocalStack (docker stop localstack).

solution.text:
jq '.InstanceType = "m8i.2xlarge" | .TagSpecifications[0].Tags[1].Value = "full"' lt.json > lt-full.json
aws ec2 create-launch-template --launch-template-name ai-agents-sandbox-full \
  --launch-template-data file://lt-full.json \
  --query 'LaunchTemplate.[LaunchTemplateName,LatestVersionNumber]' --output text

for size in lite full; do
  aws ec2 describe-launch-template-versions --launch-template-name ai-agents-sandbox-$size \
    --query 'LaunchTemplateVersions[0].LaunchTemplateData.[InstanceType,MetadataOptions.HttpTokens,MetadataOptions.HttpPutResponseHopLimit]' \
    --output text
done
# m8i.xlarge   required  1
# m8i.2xlarge  required  1

curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \
  http://localhost:1338/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ai-agent-sandbox | jq .Expiration

lab.fix:
A teammate opened a pull request with a template for the wide size. Save it as lt-wide.json:
{
  "ImageId": "resolve:ssm:/ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id",
  "InstanceType": "m8i.4xlarge",
  "IamInstanceProfile": { "Name": "ai-agent-sandbox" },
  "NetworkInterfaces": [{ "DeviceIndex": 0, "AssociatePublicIpAddress": true }],
  "MetadataOptions": { "HttpTokens": "optional", "HttpPutResponseHopLimit": 2, "HttpEndpoint": "enabled" },
  "BlockDeviceMappings": [{ "DeviceName": "/dev/sda1", "Ebs": { "VolumeType": "gp3", "VolumeSize": 120, "Encrypted": true } }],
  "TagSpecifications": [{ "ResourceType": "instance", "Tags": [{ "Key": "ai-agents:managed", "Value": "true" }, { "Key": "ai-agents:size", "Value": "wide" }] }]
}
They say the test containers "needed to read the region from the metadata service", and that a public address "makes debugging easier". Find the three settings that break the rules from this lesson with jq '{meta: .MetadataOptions, net: .NetworkInterfaces}' lt-wide.json. To see what the first one costs, edit imds.json to "imdsv2": false, restart the mock (docker rm -f imds, then the docker run from step 5), and run the plain GET from step 6 without -o /dev/null: the mock now hands the credentials to anyone who asks. Then repair lt-wide.json, put imds.json back to true, and create ai-agents-sandbox-wide.
explain: Why do we write the metadata rules in the launch template instead of configuring each VM after it starts?
A test helper that only follows URLs gets 401 from the metadata service. What does a program need to do that the helper cannot?
Hop limit 1 stops containers on the VM from getting a token. Why is that not enough on its own, and what is the real wall behind it?
lab.done: Both templates require tokens with hop limit 1, the plain GET gets 401 while the token flow works, and the mock and LocalStack are stopped.

check.q: Why does every sandbox VM start from a launch template instead of a long run-instances command?

options.text: Because AWS cannot start a VM without one
options.why: You can start a VM with only command-line options. The template is about sameness, not about what AWS requires.

options.text: Because a launch template starts VMs faster
options.why: Speed comes from the warm pool. The template only stores the answers to the launch questions.

options.text: Because the rules written there, like IMDSv2 and the near-empty role, then hold for every VM without anyone repeating them
options.why: The warm pools and the image test launch only from the templates, so one file sets the rules for all sandbox VMs.

check.q: With HttpTokens set to required, what must a program on the VM do to read the role's credentials?

options.text: Send a PUT to get a token, then send the token in a header with each GET
options.why: That is the IMDSv2 flow. A program that can only follow a URL cannot do the PUT with its special header.
The user does not matter to IMDS itself; on our image a firewall rule even blocks the agent user. The token is what IMDS checks.

options.text: Use an SSH key from the launch template
options.why: The sandbox templates have no SSH key, and IMDS never asks for one.

check.q: A teammate sets the hop limit to 2 so a test container can read the region from the metadata service. What else does that change?

options.text: Nothing else, the region is harmless
options.why: The hop limit does not care what the container asks for. Once the token reaches it, every path is open, the credentials included.

options.text: Any container on the VM can now get a token and read the role's credentials
options.why: A container is one hop further than the VM. Hop limit 1 is what keeps the token from reaching it.

options.text: The VM can now be reached from the internet
options.why: The hop limit only affects the metadata service's replies. Reachability comes from routes and security groups.

p: The infrastructure repo holds one launch template per size, lite, full and wide, all in one module next to the warm pools. Each boots the image found in the SSM parameter /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id, requires IMDSv2 with hop limit 1, gets an encrypted gp3 disk, no public address, the sandbox security group and the near-empty instance role, and tags the VM and its disk with ai-agents:managed=true and its size.

The image itself, ai-agent-sandbox, is built with Packer and Ansible, and its host rules keep the metadata address for root only. A nightly workflow builds it, boots it from the full template, runs a smoke test, and only then writes the new image ID into the parameter; the previous ID stays in a second parameter for a one-command rollback.

tickets.why: The three launch templates with IMDSv2, hop limit 1, the encrypted disk, no public address and the near-empty role.
The ai-agent-sandbox image and its host rules that keep the metadata address away from the agent and from containers.
The nightly build, smoke test and promotion through the SSM parameter.

words.plain: The size of an EC2 machine, like m8i.2xlarge: family, generation, processor and size.
Amazon Machine Image: the saved disk a VM boots from, with the system and tools installed.
A saved set of answers for starting a VM: image, size, role, disk, metadata rules and tags.
The instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254, which tells a VM about itself and hands out its role's credentials.
The version of IMDS that answers only requests carrying a token from a PUT request.
How many network hops the token reply may travel; 1 keeps it on the VM and away from containers.

review.q: Write the MetadataOptions block of a sandbox launch template from memory, and say what each of the two important lines prevents.
review.a: HttpTokens required (a plain GET, such as one from a tricked URL fetcher, gets 401) and HttpPutResponseHopLimit 1 (the token never reaches a container); HttpEndpoint enabled, InstanceMetadataTags disabled.

review.q: Why does the launch template name an SSM parameter instead of an AMI ID?
review.a: So promoting a new nightly image, or rolling back to the previous one, is one write to the parameter, and no template has to change.

review.q: Name the three sandbox sizes and what each one is for.
review.a: lite (m8i.xlarge) for plans and small routines, full (m8i.2xlarge) for builds with the whole product, wide (m8i.4xlarge) for the heaviest work.

remember: Every sandbox VM is born from a launch template, so its rules hold for all of them, and the most important rule is IMDSv2 with hop limit 1: no token, no credentials.
